chapters.title: Chapter 2: Economic Terms an Angel Must Negotiate

lessons.title: Conversion Rights and Mandatory Conversion Triggers

children.text: Rohan holds 625 CCPS and has always assumed that, whenever conversion happens, each one simply turns into one equity share. He is about to learn two things at once: conversion does not always happen when he expects, and it does not always happen at exactly 1:1 either.

body.text: Conversion is the moment a CCPS stops being a preference share, with all the protections that come with it, and becomes an ordinary equity share. When that moment happens, and how many equity shares each CCPS actually becomes, are both negotiated terms, not fixed facts.

children.text: Every CCPS term sheet distinguishes between conversion the investor chooses and conversion that happens whether the investor wants it or not.

columns.label: Optional (Investor-Elected)
points: The investor can convert to equity at any time, by choice
Almost never exercised early, since preference rights are usually worth more unconverted
One-way: once converted to equity, there is no converting back to CCPS
Useful mainly when voting as equity matters more than a preference an investor is confident they will not need

columns.label: Mandatory (Automatic)
points: Conversion happens automatically once a defined trigger occurs, no election needed
Cannot be blocked by an individual investor once the trigger is met
Typical triggers: an IPO, a qualifying new financing round, majority consent of the CCPS class, or a fixed long-stop date
Exists to stop preference shares from indefinitely complicating the cap table

children.text: "Clause 22, Conversion (illustrative wording): Each CCPS shall automatically and mandatorily convert into one (1) fully paid-up Equity Share, subject to adjustment in accordance with the anti-dilution provisions of the Shareholders' Agreement, upon the earliest of: (a) immediately prior to the filing of the red herring prospectus for a Qualified IPO; (b) the written consent of holders of not less than 75% of the then-outstanding CCPS; or (c) the date falling 20 (twenty) years from the date of issuance."

body.caption: The four mandatory conversion triggers packed into Clause 22

cells: All CCPS convert to equity before the offer document is filed
Exchanges require a single class of equity to list; preference shares cannot remain outstanding
A future round above an agreed size or valuation can trigger conversion
Keeps the cap table clean for a large new investor coming in
If enough CCPS holders agree, every CCPS in the class converts, including holdouts
Stops a small minority investor from blocking an exit or restructuring
Conversion happens automatically on this date regardless of any other event
Gives the instrument a hard expiry so it cannot sit unconverted forever

children.text: Why the IPO Trigger Is Non-Negotiable

Of the four triggers in Clause 22, only one is not really up for negotiation. SEBI's public issue regulations require a company to convert all outstanding preference shares and other convertible securities into equity before it can file its offer document. There is no version of an Indian IPO where CCPS holders keep their preference rights and list alongside everyone else.

body.text: This is why the majority-consent and long-stop triggers matter more in practice than the IPO trigger. An IPO forces conversion anyway. The other two exist for every outcome that is not an IPO: an acquisition, a later financing round, or simply the passage of time with no exit at all.

children.text: Conversion Ratio: Usually 1:1, Until It Isn't
Clause 22 says each CCPS converts into one equity share, "subject to adjustment." The number of equity shares one CCPS converts into is its
, and it is fixed at 1:1 only until something changes the

markDefs.definition: The number of equity shares each preferred share converts into. Set at 1:1 when issued, but adjustable by anti-dilution protection.
The price used to calculate how many equity shares a preferred share converts into. Starts equal to the original issue price and can be lowered by anti-dilution protection.

body.latex: \text{Conversion Ratio} = \frac{\text{Original Issue Price}}{\text{Conversion Price}}, \qquad \text{Equity Shares Received} = \text{CCPS Held} \times \text{Conversion Ratio}
body.caption: When the conversion price is adjusted downward, the ratio rises above 1, and each CCPS converts into more than one equity share.

children.text: Suppose a future down round forces ChaiCart's anti-dilution formula to adjust Rohan's conversion price from ₹3,200 down to ₹2,560. His conversion ratio becomes ₹3,200 ÷ ₹2,560 = 1.25, and his 625 CCPS would convert into 625 × 1.25 = 781.25 equity shares instead of 625. Companies typically round fractional shares down and pay cash for the leftover fraction, or round according to their Articles.

body.text: This adjustable conversion ratio is not a separate feature. It is the actual mechanism anti-dilution protection uses to compensate an investor for a lower-priced later round, which the next lesson covers in full.

body.title: Adjusting the Ratio
body.prompt: If ChaiCart's anti-dilution formula instead adjusts Rohan's conversion price from ₹3,200 down to ₹2,000, how many total equity shares would his 625 CCPS convert into?
body.explanation: Conversion ratio = ₹3,200 ÷ ₹2,000 = 1.6. Equity shares received = 625 × 1.6 = 1,000. A lower conversion price always means more equity shares for the same number of CCPS.

children.text: Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 caps how long a company can keep redeemable preference shares outstanding, generally 20 years. A CCPS is not redeemable, it must convert rather than be repaid in cash, so this statutory cap does not directly bind it. Even so, most Indian term sheets still write in a long-stop conversion date of their own, commonly somewhere in the 15 to 20 year range, simply so the instrument cannot sit unconverted on the cap table indefinitely.

body.label: Why a long-stop date exists even without a legal requirement
body.context: A CCPS that never converts is an odd, permanent fixture on a cap table: neither exited nor equity. Term sheets set a long-stop date to guarantee the instrument eventually resolves one way or another, independent of whether the law technically forces it.

body.title: The Reluctant Holdout
body.scenario: ChaiCart is preparing for an IPO. Separately, 80% of its Series A CCPS holders, by value, have already given written consent to convert their CCPS to equity ahead of a large new financing round the company wants to close first. Rohan, holding a small stake, would prefer to keep his CCPS unconverted a little longer, since he is nervous about the new round's pricing.
body.prompt: Can Rohan refuse to convert? Does it matter that an IPO is also coming?
body.modelAnswer: No, not under Clause 22 as drafted. Once holders of at least 75% of the CCPS class consent, every CCPS in that class converts automatically, including Rohan's, whatever his personal preference. The 80% threshold here clears that bar. It would not have mattered either way once the IPO itself gets close: SEBI's listing requirements would force conversion before the offer document is filed, with or without a majority-consent clause. The majority-consent trigger matters precisely for situations like this one, a financing round short of an actual IPO, where the law itself would not otherwise force conversion.

body.title: Negotiable or Not
body.question: Which one of Clause 22's four conversion triggers is genuinely not open to negotiation between ChaiCart and Rohan?
options: Conversion immediately before an IPO's offer document is filed
Whether a Qualified Financing round triggers conversion at all
body.explanation: The majority-consent threshold, the long-stop date, and whether a financing round triggers conversion are all drafting choices, negotiated deal by deal. Pre-IPO conversion is not: it follows directly from SEBI's requirement that a company list a single class of equity, so no term sheet can negotiate around it.

cards.definition: Conversion an investor chooses to trigger voluntarily, at any time, which is one-way and rarely exercised early.
Conversion that happens automatically once a defined trigger occurs, such as an IPO, a qualified financing round, majority consent, or a long-stop date.
The number of equity shares one preferred share converts into. Set at 1:1 initially, and adjustable through anti-dilution protection.
The price used to calculate the conversion ratio. Starts equal to the original issue price and can be lowered by anti-dilution protection, raising the ratio.
A fixed date, commonly 15 to 20 years after issuance, on which conversion happens automatically regardless of any other trigger.
A clause forcing every share in a class to convert once a defined majority, such as 75%, consents, preventing a small holdout from blocking the outcome.

points: Conversion is when a CCPS stops being a preference share and becomes ordinary equity, giving up its preference in exchange for full upside and voting rights.
Optional conversion is the investor's choice and is rarely used early. Mandatory conversion happens automatically once a defined trigger occurs.
Pre-IPO conversion is not negotiable: SEBI's listing rules require a single class of equity, so all CCPS must convert before the offer document is filed.
Majority-consent and long-stop-date triggers matter most for the non-IPO outcomes: financing rounds, acquisitions, or simply time passing with no exit.
The conversion ratio is usually 1:1 but can rise above 1 when the conversion price is adjusted downward, which is exactly how anti-dilution protection is implemented mechanically.
A long-stop conversion date, though not always legally required for a CCPS, is written into most term sheets anyway to guarantee the instrument eventually resolves.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or investment advice. ChaiCart and Rohan are fictional and used for illustration, and the clause language and thresholds shown are illustrative rather than a template for a real transaction. Conversion mechanics, regulatory requirements and rounding treatment for fractional shares vary by deal and change with market practice, and should be reviewed by a qualified lawyer before you rely on them. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid, and can result in the loss of your entire capital.
